claims.claim: Retinotopic maps were compared to chemoarchitectonic borders via cytochrome C oxidase-stained tangential sections of flattened cortex from 4 Emx1-Ai96 mice.
claims.source: To compare retinotopic and chemoarchitectonic borders, after retinotopic mapping we processed tissue for cytochrome C oxidase staining. We labeled surface vasculature with a fluorescent dye by transcardial perfusion immediately before fixation, used the vasculature to align images acquired in vivo (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), after fixation (whole mount, Figure 4B), after flattening (Figure 4C) and after sectioning parallel to the cortical surface and staining (Figure 4D) and compared retinotopic and chemoarchitectonic borders from 4 Emx1-Ai96 mice (Figure 4G–J).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach for comparing borders.

claims.claim: The retinotopic map extends into primary somatosensory cortex and retrosplenial cortex.
claims.source: The results confirm that the retinotopic map extends into primary somatosensory cortex and retrosplenial cortex (Figure 4G–I), with RLL mapping to the posterior whiskers (posterior barrels) of barrel columns B and C.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the comparison of retinotopic and chemoarchitectonic borders.

claims.claim: RLL maps to the posterior whiskers (posterior barrels) of barrel columns B and C.
claims.source: The results confirm that the retinotopic map extends into primary somatosensory cortex and retrosplenial cortex (Figure 4G–I), with RLL mapping to the posterior whiskers (posterior barrels) of barrel columns B and C.
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding about the anatomical location of RLL.

claims.claim: The lateral border of chemoarchitectonically-defined V1 runs through functionally-defined areas RL and LM.
claims.source: Another prominent feature of the comparison between cytochrome oxidase-based chemoarchitectonic and GCaMP6-based functional maps is a mismatch in the location of the lateral border of V1. The lateral border of chemoarchitectonically-defined V1 runs through functionally-defined areas RL and LM.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the comparison of borders.

claims.claim: The distance between the chemoarchitectonically-defined lateral border of V1 and that defined by functional retinotopy, measured along the LM/RL border, was 312 ± 88 µm in 4 Emx1-Ai96 mice.
claims.source: The distance between the chemoarchitectonically-defined lateral border of V1 and that defined by functional retinotopy, measured along the LM/RL border, was 312 ± 88 µm (4 Emx1-Ai96 mice).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of the border mismatch.

claims.claim: One possible explanation for the mismatch is that the cytochrome oxidase-rich region of visual cortex extends beyond the reversal in retinotopy that defines the functional border of V1.
claims.source: One possible explanation for the mismatch is that the cytochrome oxidase-rich region of visual cortex extends beyond the reversal in retinotopy that defines the functional border of V1.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed mismatch.

claims.claim: Misalignment on the scale of the observed mismatch is unlikely given the fluorescent marker-based registration process and direct alignment of images from live and fixed tissue.
claims.source: Alternatively, the apparent mismatch in border locations might be an experimental artifact arising from misalignment of the maps during fixation and subsequent histological processing, but misalignment on this scale is unlikely given our fluorescent marker-based registration process and direct alignment of images from live and fixed tissue.
claims.evidence: This is an argument against an alternative explanation based on the experimental methods.

claims.claim: Cytoarchitectonic borders were identified in Rorb-Ai93 mice.

claims.evidence: This is a statement about the expression pattern of the Rorb line with citation to a database.

claims.source: Consequently, GCaMP6 fluorescence-based retinotopic maps were inherently aligned to cytoarchitectonic borders in Rorb-Ai93 mice, eliminating the potential for misalignment resulting from tissue processing.

claims.claim: Comparison of cytoarchitectonic and functional retinotopic borders in Rorb-Ai93 mice indicated a mismatch, with the lateral border of cytoarchitectonically-defined V1 being lateral of the functionally-defined border and running through functionally-defined areas RL and LM.

claims.evidence: This is a primary finding confirming the border mismatch in a different experimental system.

claims.claim: The distance between the cytoarchitectonically-defined lateral border of V1 and that defined by functional retinotopy, measured along the LM/RL border, was 120 ± 38 µm in 10 Rorb-Ai93 mice.

claims.claim: The change in fluorescence at borders was less pronounced in Emx1-Ai93 mice than in Rorb-Ai93 mice.

claims.claim: Borders were visible after averaging images of the resting GCaMP6 fluorescence from 10 Emx1-Ai93 mice.

claims.evidence: This describes the method for visualizing borders in Emx1-Ai93 mice.

claims.claim: In Emx1-Ai93 mice, the lateral border of cytoarchitectonically-defined V1 was lateral of the functionally-defined border of V1 by 236 µm (measured along the LM/RL border).
claims.source: Here again, the lateral border of cytoarchitectonically-defined V1 was lateral of the functionally-defined border of V1 (Figure 5F), by 236 µm (measured along the LM/RL border).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of the border mismatch.

claims.claim: Three methods have been particularly influential in the generation of established maps of the mouse visual cortex: architectonics, functional retinotopy, and projection-based retinotopy.
claims.source: Three methods have been particularly influential in the generation of established maps of the mouse visual cortex: architectonics, using various stains, including cytochrome oxidase; functional retinotopy, primarily measured with electrodes; and projection-based retinotopy, in which axonal projections between visual areas were used to identify locations with matching retinotopy.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of prior methodological approaches.

claims.claim: Data from the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas was used to investigate the alignment of architectonic and projection-based retinotopic borders.
claims.source: To investigate the alignment of architectonic and projection-based retinotopic borders, we used data from the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas (Oh et al., 2014; http://connectivity.brain-map.org/).
claims.evidence: This describes the data source with citation.

claims.claim: Projection data from 99 mice, each with a single injection of anterograde fluorescent tracer into V1, was selected.
claims.source: We selected projection data from 99 mice, each with a single injection of anterograde fluorescent tracer into V1.
claims.evidence: This describes the data selection criteria.

claims.claim: The injections and resulting projection maps were registered to a three-dimensional reference atlas of the mouse brain built from serial section image data sets from 1675 mice.
claims.source: These injections, and the resulting projection maps, were registered to a three-dimensional reference atlas of the mouse brain built from serial section image data sets from 1675 mice.
claims.evidence: This describes the registration process with reference to the atlas.

claims.claim: The reference atlas includes tissue autofluorescence images in which major cytoarchitectonic areas are readily visible in the top projection.
claims.source: The reference atlas includes tissue autofluorescence images and in the top projection, the major cytoarchitectonic areas (including primary visual cortex, whisker and digit barrels in primary sensory cortex, primary auditory cortex and retrosplenial cortex) are readily visible (Figure 6A) due to the enhanced autofluorescence of regions with increased myelination.
claims.evidence: This describes a feature of the reference atlas.

claims.claim: Major cytoarchitectonic areas are readily visible in the top projection due to the enhanced autofluorescence of regions with increased myelination.
claims.source: The reference atlas includes tissue autofluorescence images and in the top projection, the major cytoarchitectonic areas (including primary visual cortex, whisker and digit barrels in primary sensory cortex, primary auditory cortex and retrosplenial cortex) are readily visible (Figure 6A) due to the enhanced autofluorescence of regions with increased myelination.
claims.evidence: This explains the basis for the visibility of architectonic borders.

claims.claim: LLA appears to extend into auditory cortex based on projection-based mapping.
claims.source: LLA also appears to extend into auditory cortex.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the projection-based mapping analysis.

claims.claim: The myeloarchitectonically-defined lateral border of V1 was lateral to the lateral border of V1 defined by projection-based retinotopy.
claims.source: Regarding the relative positions of the borders of V1, the myeloarchitectonically-defined lateral border of V1 (here visible as a transition between relatively bright autofluorescence in V1 and dimmer autofluorescence more laterally) was lateral to the lateral border of V1 defined by projection-based retinotopy (Figure 6E,F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of projection-based and architectonic borders.

claims.claim: The distance between the myeloarchitectonically-defined lateral border of V1 and that defined by projection-based retinotopy, measured along the LM/RL border, was 180 µm.
claims.source: The distance between the myeloarchitectonically-defined lateral border of V1 and that defined by projection-based retinotopy, measured along the LM/RL border, was 180 µm.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of the border mismatch.

claims.claim: Retinotopic organization extends into retrosplenial and primary somatosensory cortices in the mouse.
claims.source: The above comparisons of retinotopic maps with architectonic borders using three different methods lead us to two main conclusions. Firstly, retinotopic organization extends into retrosplenial and primary somatosensory cortices in the mouse.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by multiple lines of evidence.

claims.claim: RLL is entirely within barrel cortex.
claims.source: RLL is entirely within barrel cortex.

claims.claim: The retinotopic map in retrosplenial cortex was not segmented into two distinct regions by the algorithm.
claims.source: The retinotopic map observed in retrosplenial cortex was often continuous with the map in PM, and was not segmented into two distinct regions by our algorithm.

claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by multiple measurements.

claims.source: As expected, the gradient of the relationship between somatic azimuth and distance to the border was steeper in LM than in V1, indicating greater cortical magnification in V1 than in LM near the border.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the observed gradients about cortical magnification.

claims.claim: The lowest-azimuth bin was centered at −30 µm, indicating that the single-cell border was 30 µm lateral of the widefield retinotopic border.
claims.source: The lowest-azimuth bin was centered at −30 µm, indicating that the single-cell border was 30 µm lateral of the widefield retinotopic border.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of the difference in border locations.

claims.source: In addition to the new field sign patches and medial displacement of the lateral border of V1, GCaMP6 fluorescence-based retinotopic maps differ from previous maps in two respects. Firstly, area P extends across the posterior border of V1, from LM to PM.
claims.evidence: This describes a difference from prior maps.

claims.claim: Area M is displaced medially relative to the location reported in Garrett et al. (2014).
claims.source: Secondly, area M is displaced medially relative to the location reported in Garrett et al. (2014).
claims.evidence: This describes a difference from a prior study with citation.

claims.source: One result of these differences is an almost continuous ring of field sign positive areas surrounding V1, broken only by the field sign negative area AM.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the overall organization of visual areas.

claims.evidence: This is a specific observation about the visual field bias of LM.

claims.claim: RL was biased towards the lower nasal visual field.
claims.source: The 4 positive field sign patches around V1 (LM, RL, PM, P; Figure 8A) each represented a portion of the visual field and each was biased towards a different quadrant: LM was biased towards the upper nasal visual field, RL the lower nasal field, P upper temporal field and PM lower temporal field (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is a specific observation about the visual field bias of RL.

claims.claim: P was biased towards the upper temporal visual field.

claims.evidence: This is a specific observation about the visual field bias of P.

claims.claim: PM was biased towards the lower temporal visual field.

claims.evidence: This is a specific observation about the visual field bias of PM.

claims.claim: The summed coverage of the four patches (LM, RL, PM, P) approximated that of V1 with modest overlap in coverage in two narrow strips of visual space.
claims.source: The summed coverage of these four patches approximated that of V1 with modest overlap in coverage in two narrow strips of visual space ~0–15° above the horizon and ~40–50° from the vertical meridian.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the combined visual field coverage.

claims.claim: The center of coverage of V1 was at altitude 7.4 ± 2.1 degrees, azimuth 37.8 ± 1.4 degrees (14 mice).
claims.source: The intersection of these zones of overlap included the center of coverage of V1 (altitude 7.4 ± 2.1 degrees, azimuth 37.8 ± 1.4 degrees, 14 mice), which was represented in areas LM, RL and PM.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of the center of V1 coverage.

claims.claim: The center of coverage of V1 was represented in areas LM, RL and PM.
claims.source: The intersection of these zones of overlap included the center of coverage of V1 (altitude 7.4 ± 2.1 degrees, azimuth 37.8 ± 1.4 degrees, 14 mice), which was represented in areas LM, RL and PM.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the overlap in visual field coverage.

claims.claim: The arrangement of early visual areas in the mouse resembles that in primates, where V1 is surrounded by V2.
claims.source: A prominent feature of GCaMP6-based retinotopic maps is the four positive field sign areas (RL, LM, P and PM) neighboring V1 that form an almost continuous ring, broken only by the negative field sign area AM. This arrangement resembles early visual areas in primates, in which V1 is a negative field sign region surrounded by V2, and V2 is a continuous strip of positive field sign tissue broken only at a single point (anterior tip of the calcarine sulcus; Gattass et al., 2005; Sereno et al., 1995; Warnking et al., 2002; Silver and Kastner, 2009; Wilms et al., 2010; Laumann et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative observation with citations to primate studies.

claims.claim: Early studies of mouse visual cortex revealed a retinotopic map in V1 and a second map anterior and lateral to V1, leading this second region to be named V2.
claims.source: Early studies of mouse visual cortex revealed a retinotopic map in V1 and a second map anterior and lateral to V1, leading this second region to be named V2 (Wagor et al., 1980).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the history of mouse visual cortex mapping with citation.

claims.claim: Further studies revealed several overlapping maps within mouse and rat V2, which was therefore split into several named visual areas, including LM and RL.
claims.source: Further studies revealed several overlapping maps within mouse and rat V2, which was therefore split into several named visual areas, including LM and RL (Olavarria and Montero, 1981, 1984, 1989; Malach, 1989; Olavarria et al., 1982; Thomas and Espinoza, 1987; Coogan and Burkhalter, 1993; Wang and Burkhalter, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the evolution of understanding of mouse visual areas with citations.

claims.claim: The visual field representations of the four areas around V1 (LM, P, PM, RL) are complementary, with the outline of the coverage of these four areas matching the outline of V1 coverage.
claims.source: Our results indicate that the visual field representations of the four areas around V1 (LM, P, PM, RL) are complementary, with the outline of the coverage of these four areas matching the outline of V1 coverage.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the visual field coverage analysis.

claims.claim: The results likely underestimate the range of visual coverage in each area and the overlap between areas.
claims.source: Our results likely underestimate the range of visual coverage in each area and the overlap between areas.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the measurements.

claims.claim: V1 included a visual coverage range of ~60° in altitude and ~90° in azimuth, comparable to measurements with reflectance-based imaging but smaller than the range measured with single-cell electrical recordings.
claims.source: V1 included a visual coverage range of ~60° in altitude and ~90° in azimuth, comparable to measurements with reflectance-based imaging (e.g. Garrett et al., 2014) but smaller than the range measured with single-cell electrical recordings (~100° in altitude and ~150° in azimuth; Wagor et al. (1980).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative statement about visual field coverage with citations.

claims.claim: Single-cell recordings are likely to provide a larger range of visual coverage than widefield mapping for two main reasons.
claims.source: Single-cell recordings are likely to provide a larger range for two main reasons.
claims.evidence: This introduces an explanation for the difference in coverage measurements.

claims.source: Firstly, widefield mapping identifies retinotopic position based on the peak of activity, thereby emphasizing the receptive field center.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation of a methodological difference.

claims.claim: The outer limits at which visual stimuli can evoke activity in V1 will be expanded by approximately the radius of the largest receptive fields of neurons at the edges of V1.
claims.source: The outer limits at which visual stimuli can evoke activity in V1 will be expanded, by approximately the radius of the largest receptive fields of neurons at the edges of V1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about how receptive field size affects coverage estimates.

claims.claim: A more pronounced expansion in effective coverage is expected in higher visual areas, where receptive field sizes are larger.
claims.source: A more pronounced expansion in effective coverage is expected in higher visual areas, where receptive field sizes are larger (Wang and Burkhalter, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is an inference with citation to prior measurements of receptive field sizes.

claims.claim: Widefield fluorescence measures the average retinotopy of the local population of neurons.
claims.source: Secondly, widefield fluorescence measures the average retinotopy of the local population of neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the nature of widefield measurements.

claims.claim: Single-cell receptive field centers vary around the mean retinotopy.
claims.source: Single-cell receptive field centers vary around the mean retinotopy.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about variability in single-cell measurements.

claims.claim: In V1, most pyramidal neuron receptive fields are within ~7 degrees of the local population average.
claims.source: For example, in V1 most pyramidal neuron receptive fields are within ~7 degrees of the local population average (Bonin et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about receptive field scatter with citation.

claims.claim: No higher visual areas (even those immediately surrounding V1) contain a complete description of the visual hemifield.
claims.source: Even allowing for some expansion of coverage for each visual area, our results indicate that no higher visual areas (even those immediately surrounding V1) contain a complete description of the visual hemifield.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the coverage analysis.

claims.claim: Information on features that subtend more than approximately a quarter of the visual field will be routed to different early visual areas.
claims.source: Hence information on features that subtend more than approximately a quarter of the visual field will be routed to different early visual areas, with the result that information on features in different locations within a single visual scene will be processed in regions with different functional properties.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the coverage patterns.

results.result: GCaMP6 reporter mice (Ai95, Ai96, Ai93) crossed with Emx1-IRES-Cre were used for fluorescence imaging through a 5 mm cranial window, with all three lines showing significantly greater baseline fluorescence than wild-type mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C14, C20-C27 describe the experimental setup and baseline fluorescence measurements. The quantitative data (C25-C27) showing 10.3±1.3, 4.7±0.5, and 49.7±5.9 fold increases over wild-type are specific and supported by Figure 1H. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate controls.

results.result: All three GCaMP6 mouse lines displayed larger amplitude and faster kinetics of fluorescence changes compared to wild-type autofluorescence, with Emx1-Ai93 showing the largest response (10±2.4% ΔF/F, 216× wild-type) and fastest kinetics (219±60 ms latency to peak).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C47 provide comprehensive quantitative characterization of GCaMP6 responses across three mouse lines with appropriate wild-type controls. The data show consistent patterns with detailed kinetic measurements (latency, rise time, decay time) for each line. Statistical measures (mean±SEM, ranges, sample sizes) are provided throughout.

results.result: Retinotopic maps were generated using a spherically-corrected drifting checkerboard stimulus (0.043-0.048 Hz) in awake, head-restrained mice, with 10-40 stimulus presentations averaged per direction and automated border identification using a manually-tuned threshold (mean 0.32±0.004).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C59 describe the retinotopic mapping methodology with appropriate detail. The stimulus parameters, averaging procedures, and analysis pipeline are clearly specified. The threshold robustness analysis (C57, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) demonstrates that results are stable across the parameter range employed (0.2-0.4).

results.result: Eye movements during mapping were characterized (up to 5-10° vertical, 15-20° horizontal), but with mean displacement <1° and movements occurring during all stimulus phases, the effects were eliminated by averaging. A constant mean luminance stimulus was used to minimize pupil size changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 address a critical potential confound with appropriate measurements and controls. The eye tracking data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) support the conclusion that averaging eliminates movement artifacts. The constant luminance design (C64) and pupil measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) provide additional validation.

results.result: Most field sign patches were visible after only 15 minutes of imaging (10 sweeps per direction), maps were stable across imaging sessions, and displayed consistent structure across mice, representing a practical advantage over prior reflectance-based methods requiring 1-2 hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 demonstrate the efficiency and reproducibility of the GCaMP6 method. The 15-minute mapping time (C71) is supported by Figure 3A, stability across sessions is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 (C72), and the comparison to prior methods (C73) is appropriately cited to Garrett et al. 2014.

results.result: GCaMP6 fluorescence mapping revealed three new field sign patches: MMA and MMP (medial to AM and PM in the MM region) appeared consistently across mice (>85% incidence, significant k-means clusters), while RLL (anterior-lateral to RL) was less consistent (60% incidence, non-significant cluster).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C16, C76, C80-C81, C83-C84, C107, C111-C112, C116 describe the identification of new retinotopic patches. The consistency of MMA and MMP is supported by multiple metrics: appearance in mean field sign map (C84), high incidence (C94, C111), and significant k-means clustering (C109, C111). RLL shows lower consistency (C106, C110, C112) but still appears in the mean map.

results.result: Across 14 mice (4 Emx1-Ai96, 10 Emx1-Ai93), the maximum number of field sign patches in individual maps was 9 positive and 7 negative, with 10 patches (V1, LM, LI, AL, RL, AM, PM, MMA, MMP, P) occurring in >85% of mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C89, C94 provide quantitative summary of mapping results across mice. The data show consistency between mouse lines (C87-C89) and identify highly reproducible patches (C94). Sample sizes are appropriate (14 mice total) and the quantitative metrics are clearly stated.

results.result: The ability to map additional regions of retinotopic organization likely results from the superior signal-to-noise ratio of GCaMP6, as the newly identified patches (MMA, MMP, RLL, LLA) showed smaller fluorescence changes than established visual areas, with RLL showing the weakest activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114, C117-C118 provide a mechanistic explanation for the discovery of new patches. The hypothesis (C113) is supported by quantitative data showing smaller amplitude responses in the new patches (C114, Figure 3F), with RLL showing the smallest changes (C117), consistent with its lower mapping consistency (C118).

results.result: The newly identified field sign patches extend >2 mm beyond V1 borders, likely extending into architectonically-defined retrosplenial cortex (medial extension of PM) and barrel cortex (RLL and possibly RL), based on anatomical constraints.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C125 make anatomical inferences about the location of new patches. The >2 mm extent (C119) is a quantitative observation. The inferences about retrosplenial (C122-C123) and barrel cortex (C124-C125) are reasonable based on known anatomical boundaries, though these remain inferences pending direct confirmation.

results.result: Comparison of retinotopic maps to chemoarchitectonic borders (cytochrome oxidase staining, 4 Emx1-Ai96 mice) confirmed that retinotopic organization extends into primary somatosensory cortex (with RLL mapping to posterior barrels B and C) and retrosplenial cortex, with a mismatch of 312±88 μm between chemoarchitectonic and functional V1 borders.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C126-C130, C155-C156 describe a major finding using careful registration methods (fluorescent vasculature labeling, Figure 4). The extension into barrel cortex is directly demonstrated (C127-C128), and the border mismatch is quantified (C130). The registration approach addresses potential alignment artifacts (C132).

results.result: Using Rorb-Ai93 mice where cytoarchitectonic borders are inherently aligned with functional maps (eliminating tissue processing artifacts), the lateral V1 border mismatch was confirmed at 120±38 μm (10 mice), with the cytoarchitectonic border running through functionally-defined RL and LM.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C139 provide independent confirmation of the border mismatch using a different approach that eliminates potential registration artifacts (C137). The Rorb expression pattern (C134, cited to Allen Brain Atlas) provides the basis for this method. The mismatch magnitude (139 μm, C139) is smaller than with CO staining but in the same direction.

results.result: In Emx1-Ai93 mice, cytoarchitectonic borders were visible after averaging resting GCaMP6 fluorescence from 10 mice, showing a V1 border mismatch of 236 μm, consistent with the Rorb-Ai93 and cytochrome oxidase results.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C143 provide a third independent measurement of the border mismatch using averaged Emx1-Ai93 fluorescence. The mismatch magnitude (236 μm, C143) is intermediate between the CO staining (312 μm) and Rorb-Ai93 (120 μm) measurements, supporting the consistency of this finding across methods.

results.result: Analysis of projection-based retinotopy from the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas (99 mice with V1 injections, registered to a 3D reference atlas from 1675 mice) showed that the myeloarchitectonic V1 border was 180 μm lateral to the projection-based retinotopic border, and that LLA extends into auditory cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C154 provide a fourth independent assessment of the border mismatch using a large dataset and different methodology (projection-based retinotopy). The 180 μm mismatch (C154) is consistent with the other three measurements (mean 212 μm across all four methods, C160). The extension of LLA into auditory cortex (C152) is an additional finding.

results.result: There is a consistent mismatch between architectonic and retinotopic V1 borders across three methods (chemoarchitectonic, cytoarchitectonic, myeloarchitectonic), with the architectonic border lateral to the retinotopic border by up to ~300 μm (mean 212 μm across four measurements: 312, 120, 236, 180 μm).
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C160 synthesize the border mismatch findings across all four measurement approaches. The consistency across methods (chemoarchitectonic, cytoarchitectonic in two mouse lines, and myeloarchitectonic) strongly supports this as a real phenomenon rather than a methodological artifact. The quantitative summary (mean 212 μm) is appropriate.

results.result: 2-photon imaging of layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron receptive fields (964 neurons, 3 experiments) at the V1-LM border showed that single-cell retinotopy reversed at the widefield-defined border, with the single-cell border only 30 μm lateral of the widefield border—insufficient to account for the 100-300 μm architectonic-retinotopic mismatch.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C173 provide critical validation that widefield and single-cell borders align closely (30 μm difference, C172), ruling out population averaging as an explanation for the architectonic mismatch (C173). The sample size (964 neurons) is substantial, and the orderly retinotopic progression (C167, C170-C171) with reversal at the widefield border (C168) strongly supports the widefield measurements.

results.result: GCaMP6 fluorescence-based maps differ from previous maps in that area P extends across the posterior border of V1 from LM to PM, and area M is displaced medially relative to Garrett et al. (2014), resulting in an almost continuous ring of positive field sign areas surrounding V1, broken only by AM.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C176 describe differences from prior maps with appropriate citation (C175). The extension of P (C174) and medial displacement of M (C175) are clearly shown in the figures. The resulting ring organization (C176) is a notable organizational feature, though the functional significance requires further investigation.

results.result: The four positive field sign patches bordering V1 (LM, RL, PM, P) display complementary representations biased toward different visual field quadrants (LM: upper nasal; RL: lower nasal; P: upper temporal; PM: lower temporal), with summed coverage approximating V1 and overlap primarily at the central hemifield (7.4±2.1° altitude, 37.8±1.4° azimuth).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C177-C185 describe the visual field coverage analysis. The complementary organization with quadrant biases (C178-C182) is clearly demonstrated in Figure 8. The quantitative center of coverage (C184) and overlap pattern (C183, C185) are well-supported by the data. This represents a comprehensive characterization of visual field representation.

results.result: The arrangement of four positive field sign areas (RL, LM, P, PM) forming an almost continuous ring around V1 (broken only by AM) resembles the primate visual system where V1 is surrounded by V2, though mouse V2 was historically split into multiple areas (LM, RL, etc.) due to overlapping maps.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C189 make an interesting comparative observation with appropriate citations to primate studies (C186) and the history of mouse visual area nomenclature (C187-C188). The complementary visual field representations (C189) support this organizational similarity, though functional homology would require additional evidence.

results.result: The measured visual field coverage (V1: ~60° altitude, ~90° azimuth) likely underestimates true coverage compared to single-cell recordings (~100° altitude, ~150° azimuth) because widefield mapping emphasizes receptive field centers and measures population averages, while single cells show scatter (~7° in V1) around the local mean.
results.evaluation: Claims C190-C198 provide a thoughtful analysis of methodological differences affecting coverage estimates. The comparison to prior single-cell data (C191, cited to Wagor et al. 1980) is appropriate. The explanations based on receptive field size (C193-C195) and population averaging (C196-C198) are well-reasoned, with the scatter estimate (C198) appropriately cited to Bonin et al. 2011.

results.result: No higher visual areas (even those immediately surrounding V1) contain a complete description of the visual hemifield, meaning information on features subtending more than approximately a quarter of the visual field will be routed to different early visual areas with different functional properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C199-C200 draw an important functional inference from the coverage analysis. Even allowing for underestimation (C190), the complementary rather than redundant coverage patterns (C6, C189) support this conclusion. This has implications for understanding visual processing in mice, though the functional consequences remain to be tested experimentally.

results.result: GCaMP6 fluorescence is established as a tool for generating retinotopic maps of mouse cortex, with superior signal-to-noise ratio enabling rapid mapping and revelation of new field sign patches (MMA, MMP, RLL, RS), bringing the total to 16 distinct retinotopically-organized regions in mouse cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C201-C204 summarize the major methodological and empirical contributions. The establishment of GCaMP6 as a mapping tool (C201) is well-supported by the comprehensive characterization. The superior SNR (C202) enabled discovery of new patches (C203), and the total count of 16 regions (C8, C204) is clearly enumerated (12 published + 4 new).

results.result: Area P extends across the posterior extent of V1, consistent with prior tracer studies and recent functional maps, though signal-to-noise may be limited in this posterior region near the cranial window edge, and additional retinotopic structure may exist under the transverse sinus or in folded cortex.

results.result: Two field sign patches (MMA and MMP) were identified in the MM region between AM/PM and retrosplenial cortex, consistent with prior anatomical evidence for multiple distinct regions in MM and direct V1 projections terminating in distinct anterior and posterior regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C211-C214 connect the functional findings to prior anatomical work. The identification of MMA and MMP (C211) is well-supported by the mapping data. The consistency with prior anatomical observations (C212-C213, cited to Van der Gucht et al. 2007 and Wang and Burkhalter 2007) and the inference about correspondence (C214) strengthen the interpretation.

results.result: RLL is biased toward the nasal, lower visual field (like RL) and may convey visual information on whisker location to barrel cortex, while the visual map in retrosplenial cortex is consistent with its visual responsiveness and role in spatial memory and navigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C216-C219 make functional speculations about the newly identified patches. While the visual field bias of RLL (C216) is supported by data, the proposed function (C217) is speculative. The consistency with retrosplenial cortex function (C218-C219) is reasonable but requires experimental validation. These are plausible hypotheses for future work rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: While some areas might be activated more effectively by stimuli other than checkerboards, the broad spatial and temporal frequency content of checkerboard borders, combined with retinotopic regions occupying most territory between primary sensory areas, suggests few additional visual areas remain to be discovered and substantial differences with different stimuli would not be expected.
results.evaluation: Claims C220-C226 address potential limitations of the stimulus choice. The acknowledgment that different stimuli might activate some areas differently (C220-C222) is appropriate, but the argument that checkerboards contain broad frequency content (C223) and that most territory is already mapped (C224) provides reasonable justification for the conclusions (C225-C226).

results.result: Population imaging naturally limits resolution, and widefield fluorescence includes signals from dendrites and axons that may cross borders, yet widefield and 2-photon border locations differ by only tens of micrometers, suggesting border blurring is minimal despite these potential confounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C227-C233 provide a thoughtful discussion of methodological limitations. The acknowledgment of potential resolution limits (C227-C229) and border-crossing processes (C230-C232) is appropriate. The close agreement between widefield and 2-photon borders (C233, 30 μm difference from C172) provides empirical evidence that these concerns do not substantially affect the results.

results.result: The cellular and laminar origins of widefield GCaMP6 fluorescence remain unknown, and some observed retinotopic organization (e.g., in retrosplenial and barrel cortices) may result from retinotopically-organized axons rather than somatic retinotopy, as suggested by the lack of retinotopy in these regions in Rorb-Ai93 mice (which label layer 4/5 somata).
results.evaluation: Claims C234-C236, C90-C91 acknowledge an important limitation and provide evidence bearing on it. The lack of retinotopy in retrosplenial/barrel cortex in Rorb-Ai93 mice (C236) suggests these signals may arise from axons rather than local somata, supporting the use of 'patch' rather than 'area' terminology (C91, C237-C242). This is an appropriate interpretation of the data.

results.result: In prior architectonic-based maps, V1, AL, LM, and RL borders intersect at a common point, but retinotopic maps show the V1 border is more medial, such that V1 and AL lack a common border, with RL and LM sharing a ~100-300 μm border between them, and the architectonic V1 border running through RL and LM to intersect AL's medial tip.
results.evaluation: Claims C243-C249 explain how the border mismatch reconciles differences between prior maps. The comparison to prior architectonic maps (C243, cited to Wang and Burkhalter 2007) is appropriate. The spatial relationships described (C244-C248) follow logically from the border mismatch findings, and the interpretation that this helps explain map differences (C249) is reasonable.

results.result: The consistent mismatch between architectonic and retinotopic V1 borders across three methods indicates the architectonic border may correlate with functions other than retinotopic reversal, possibly including the binocular region (as RL and LM include binocular zone representations) or a thin monocular zone along the medial edge of LM and RL.
results.evaluation: Claims C250-C254 provide plausible hypotheses for the functional significance of the border mismatch. The consistency across methods (C250) supports that this is a real phenomenon. The proposed explanations involving binocular representation (C252-C253, cited to Wagor et al. 1980) or a monocular zone (C254, cited to Laing et al. 2015) are reasonable hypotheses that warrant future investigation.
